questions.prompt: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?

options.text: Leo said, “The game starts at six.”
Leo said “the game starts at six.”
Leo said, “The game starts at six”.

questions.explanation: A comma after the tag, a capital to start the quote, and the full stop inside the closing marks.

questions.prompt: The tag comes after the words. Which is correct?
questions.explanation: The sentence carries on into the tag, so the quote ends with a comma, not a full stop, and the comma goes inside the marks.

questions.prompt: Which question is punctuated correctly?
questions.explanation: A question mark inside the marks does the comma’s job, so don’t add a comma too.

questions.prompt: Which one is correct?
questions.explanation: The tag is still part of the same sentence, so “she” starts with a small letter, even after an exclamation mark.

questions.prompt: Mom said, “Dinner is ready” — where does the full stop go?
questions.explanation: Mom said, “Dinner is ready.” The end mark belongs to the spoken words, so it goes inside.

title: Right or needs a fix?
instructions: Check the commas, capitals and end marks. Is each line of speech punctuated right, or does it need a fix?

title: Fix the speech
instructions: Each sentence has one punctuation mistake. Rewrite it correctly. Straight quotes (") are fine.

items.task: Fix it: something is missing after the tag.
items.source: Dad said “It’s time for bed.”
hints: What goes between “said” and the quotation marks?
items.explanation: Tag first? Put a comma after the tag: Dad said, “It’s time for bed.”

items.task: Fix it: the tag comes after the words.
items.source: “I’m not tired” said Rosa.
hints: The quote needs a mark before it closes.
items.explanation: A statement before the tag ends with a comma inside the marks.

items.task: Fix it: look at the question mark.
items.source: “Where’s my phone”? asked Theo.
hints: The question mark belongs to Theo’s words.
items.explanation: The question is what Theo said, so its question mark goes inside the closing marks.

items.task: Fix it: look at the full stop.
items.source: Mr. Kim said, “Please open your books”.
answers: Mr. Kim said, “Please open your books.”
hints: Does the full stop belong to Mr. Kim’s words?
items.explanation: The full stop ends the spoken sentence, so it goes inside the closing quotation marks.

items.task: Fix it: one mark too many.
items.source: “That was amazing!,” shouted the crowd.
hints: An exclamation mark already ends the quote.
items.explanation: An exclamation mark or question mark does the comma’s job, so don’t add a comma as well.

items.task: Fix it: look at the comma.
items.source: “We won”, Jada said.
hints: Commas go inside or outside the closing marks?
items.explanation: In American English, commas and full stops always go inside the closing quotation marks.

title: Four lines of speech
prompt: Write four lines of speech from a moment at lunch, on the bus or at practice. Each line has its own task, listed above the writing box. Write them in order, and start a new line each time a different person speaks.
tips: Tag first: Kai said, “Pass the ketchup.”
Tag last: “Pass the ketchup,” Kai said. A question or exclamation keeps its mark: “Is that mine?” asked Ava.
Check every line: comma, capital, and the end mark inside the quotation marks. New speaker? New line.

sentences.ask: Someone says something, with the tag first (Name said, “…”).
Someone answers, with the tag after the words (“…,” Name said.).
Someone asks a question, with the tag after it.
Someone shouts or exclaims, with the tag first or last.

title: Where’s the tag?
instructions: Does the speech tag come before the words, after them, or in the middle (a split quote)?

items.text: Grandpa said, “Let me tell you a story.”
“I can’t find my shoe,” Max said.
“If it rains,” said Mom, “we’ll stay home.”
“I tried,” Omar sighed. “It just didn’t work.”

title: The tag that fits
instructions: Pick the speech tag that best shows how the words were spoken.

items.sentence: “Shh, the baby is sleeping,” Dad ___.
items.explanation: You don’t shout next to a sleeping baby: Dad whispered.

items.sentence: “Get off my bike!” Jamal ___.
items.explanation: The exclamation mark and the command sound loud and angry: Jamal yelled.

items.sentence: “Where did you put the remote?” Mom ___.
items.explanation: It’s a question, so “asked” fits.

items.sentence: “That’s the funniest joke ever,” Ava ___, holding her stomach.
items.explanation: A funny joke and holding her stomach: Ava laughed.

items.sentence: “I guess I’ll just stay home,” Leo ___.
items.explanation: “I guess” sounds disappointed: Leo sighed.

items.sentence: “Yes, I’ll help you,” Rosa ___.
items.explanation: Rosa is answering someone: she replied.

questions.prompt: When do you start a new paragraph in a conversation?

options.text: Every time a different person speaks
Only when you change the speech tag

questions.explanation: New speaker, new line. It lets readers follow who is talking.

questions.prompt: Which split quote is punctuated correctly?

options.text: “If we leave now,” said Kim, “We’ll be early.”
“If we leave now,” said Kim, “we’ll be early.”
“If we leave now” said Kim “we’ll be early.”

questions.explanation: It’s one sentence split by the tag, so there’s a comma on each side of the tag and the second part starts with a small letter.

questions.prompt: In “I’m tired,” said Leo_ “Let’s go home.” what goes after Leo?
questions.explanation: “Let’s go home” is a new sentence (it starts with a capital), so the tag ends with a full stop.

questions.prompt: Which line uses an action instead of a speech tag?
questions.explanation: The action (slammed the door) shows who is speaking and how she feels, with no tag at all.

questions.prompt: Why can a writer leave out some tags in a long conversation between two people?

options.text: Each new line shows that the other person is speaking.
Readers don’t care who is speaking.

questions.explanation: With a new line for every speaker, readers can keep track, so a tag every few lines is enough.

title: The great argument
prompt: Write a short scene (8–14 lines) in which two people disagree about something small: the last slice of pizza, the TV remote, whose turn it is to walk the dog. Start a new line every time the speaker changes. Use at least one tag before the words, one tag after, and one split quote.
tips: New speaker, new line: press Enter each time someone new speaks.
Split quote: “If you give me the remote,” said Kai, “I’ll do your dishes.”
Mix in an action instead of a tag: Ava crossed her arms. “No way.”

title: Exact words or reported?
instructions: Does the sentence give the speaker’s exact words (direct speech), or report what they said (reported speech)?

items.text: “We’re moving to Ohio,” Kim told us.
Ali said that he had lost his wallet.
Kim told us that they were moving to Ohio.
Ms. Moss asked if we could help.
Dad said he would be late.
The lifeguard told us not to swim.

title: One step back
instructions: Report the words. Pick the verb or pronoun that fits reported speech.

items.sentence: “I am hungry.” → Sara said that she ___ hungry.
items.explanation: am → was: the verb moves one step back.

items.sentence: “We will win.” → The team said that they ___ win.
items.explanation: will → would.

items.sentence: “I can fix it.” → Dad said that he ___ fix it.
items.explanation: can → could.

items.sentence: “They have finished.” → The coach said that they ___ finished.
items.explanation: have → had.

items.sentence: “I like your drawing.” → Maya told me that she ___ my drawing.
items.explanation: like → liked, and “your drawing” becomes “my drawing” because she was talking to me.

items.sentence: “My brother broke the vase.” → Eli said that ___ brother had broken the vase.
items.explanation: Eli’s brother: “my” becomes “his”. (And broke → had broken.)

title: Report it
instructions: Turn each line of direct speech into reported speech. No quotation marks: change the pronouns and shift the verb back. “That” is optional.

items.task: Report it.
items.source: Jay said, “I am hungry.”
answers: Jay said that he was hungry.
hints: am → was: Jay said that he was…
items.explanation: Pronoun: I → he. Verb: am → was. No quotation marks.

items.task: Report it. (Lena was talking to you.)
items.source: Lena said, “I will call you later.”
answers: Lena said that she would call me later.
Lena said she would call me later.
items.explanation: She (Lena) would call me (you, the reporter) later.

items.task: Report it. (You are in Mr. Ortiz’s class.)
items.source: Mr. Ortiz said, “We can go outside.”
answers: Mr. Ortiz said that we could go outside.
Mr. Ortiz said we could go outside.
hints: You’re in the class, so “we” stays.
items.explanation: “We” still includes you, so it stays; can → could.

items.task: Report it.
items.source: Tia said, “My cat has eaten my homework.”
answers: Tia said that her cat had eaten her homework.
Tia said her cat had eaten her homework.
items.explanation: Both “my”s become “her”, and has → had.

items.task: Report it.
items.source: The twins said, “We are tired.”
answers: The twins said that they were tired.
The twins said they were tired.
items.explanation: We → they, are → were.

items.task: Report it. (Ben was talking to you.)
items.source: Ben told me, “You are my best friend.”
answers: Ben told me that I was his best friend.
Ben told me I was his best friend.
hints: are → was (it’s about one person now).
items.explanation: You (me) → I, my (Ben’s) → his, and are → was to agree with “I”.

title: What they said
prompt: Think of four things people said to you this week (at home, at school, online). Report each one without quotation marks. Each sentence has its own task, listed above the writing box. Write them in order.
tips: Change the pronouns: “I’m late” → She said that she was late.
Shift the verb back: is → was, will → would, can → could.
No quotation marks in reported speech.

sentences.ask: Report what someone said, using “said that”.
Report something with “told” + the person (told me that…).
Report a promise or a plan: “will” becomes “would”.
Report something someone said about themselves: change “I” to he, she or they.

questions.prompt: “Where is the gym?” asked Lucas. Which report is correct?

options.text: Lucas asked where was the gym.
Lucas asked where the gym was.
Lucas asked where is the gym?

questions.explanation: Statement order (the gym was), backshift (is → was) and a full stop.

questions.prompt: “Are you coming?” Mom asked me. Which report is correct?

options.text: Mom asked me if I was coming.
Mom asked me was I coming.
Mom asked me if I was coming?

questions.explanation: A yes/no question takes “if” or “whether”, statement order, and a full stop.

questions.prompt: “Do you like jazz?” he asked her. Which report is correct?

options.text: He asked her whether she liked jazz.
He asked her whether did she like jazz.
He asked her do you like jazz.

questions.explanation: “Do” disappears; the main verb carries the tense: she liked.

questions.prompt: “Don’t be late,” Dad told me. Which report is correct?

options.text: Dad told me don’t be late.
Dad told me not to be late.
Dad told me to not being late.

questions.explanation: A “don’t” command becomes “not to” + the verb.

questions.prompt: “Please close the window,” Ms. Lin said to Ravi. Which report is correct?

options.text: Ms. Lin asked Ravi to close the window.
Ms. Lin asked Ravi close the window.
Ms. Lin asked Ravi if close the window.

questions.explanation: A polite request: asked + the person + to + the verb.

title: If, to or a question word?
instructions: Pick the word that starts the reported question or command.

items.sentence: “Is the store open?” → I asked ___ the store was open.
items.explanation: A yes/no question is reported with “if” or “whether”.

items.sentence: “Wash your hands.” → The nurse told us ___ wash our hands.
items.explanation: A command: told + the person + to + the verb.

items.sentence: “Don’t run in the hall.” → Mr. Dee told us ___ run in the hall.
items.explanation: “Don’t” becomes “not to”.

items.sentence: “Where do you live?” → She asked me ___ I lived.
items.explanation: Keep the question word, then statement order: where I lived.

items.sentence: “What are you reading?” → Grandpa asked ___ I was reading.
items.explanation: Keep “what”, then statement order: what I was reading.

items.sentence: “Can you help me?” → Ana asked ___ I could help her.
items.explanation: A yes/no question: if (or whether) I could help her.

title: Questions and commands
instructions: Report each question or command. No quotation marks, statement order for questions, a full stop at the end, and to + the verb for commands.

items.task: Report the question.
items.source: “Where is the library?” asked Tom.
answers: Tom asked where the library was.
items.explanation: Tom asked where the library was. Statement order, is → was, full stop.

items.task: Report the question. (Mia was talking to you.)
items.source: “Are you okay?” Mia asked me.
answers: Mia asked me if I was okay.
Mia asked me whether I was okay.
Mia asked if I was okay.
Mia asked whether I was okay.
hints: A yes/no question needs if or whether.
Mia asked me if I was…
items.explanation: if + statement order: I was okay.

items.task: Report the question.
items.source: “What time does the movie start?” Jo asked.
answers: Jo asked what time the movie started.
items.explanation: Without “does”, the main verb carries the tense: started.

items.task: Report the question.
items.source: “Can we have a dog?” the kids asked their parents.
answers: The kids asked their parents if they could have a dog.
The kids asked their parents whether they could have a dog.
hints: The kids asked their parents if they…
items.explanation: if + they could have: pronoun, backshift and statement order.

items.task: Report the command.
items.source: “Turn off your phones,” the teacher told us.
answers: The teacher told us to turn off our phones.
items.explanation: The teacher told us to turn off our phones.

items.task: Report the command.
items.source: “Don’t feed the ducks,” the ranger told the children.
answers: The ranger told the children not to feed the ducks.
items.explanation: The ranger told the children not to feed the ducks.

title: Interview report
prompt: Imagine you interviewed a new student, a coach or the school cook for the school website. Write a report of the interview (6–10 sentences) in reported speech, with no quotation marks. Report at least two questions you asked, their answers, and at least one piece of advice or an instruction they gave.
tips: Questions: I asked her where she had grown up. I asked if she liked our school.
Commands and advice: She told me to try the tacos. He reminded us not to forget our water bottles.
Answers: She said that she had moved from Denver.

title: Shift the time and place
instructions: The words were said days ago, somewhere else. Pick the word or words that fit the report.

items.sentence: “I’ll finish it tomorrow.” → Kim said that she would finish it ___.
items.explanation: tomorrow → the next day (the day after she spoke).

items.sentence: “I saw a fox yesterday.” → Ravi said that he had seen a fox ___.
items.explanation: yesterday → the day before.

items.sentence: “We are leaving now.” → They said that they were leaving ___.
items.explanation: now → then.

items.sentence: “Leave your coats here.” → The guide told us to leave our coats ___.
items.explanation: here → there (we aren’t in that place any more).

items.sentence: “The test is next week.” → Ms. Cho said that the test was ___.
items.explanation: next week → the following week.

items.sentence: “I love this song.” → Dee said that she loved ___ song.
items.explanation: this → that.

title: The garden report
instructions: This report was written a month after the principal spoke. Five words didn’t shift the way reported speech needs. Tap each one and fix it.
text: Last month, our principal visited our class. She said that the school is getting a new garden. She told us that the builders will start tomorrow and that every class can plant something. My friend Leo asked if he could help, and she said that he could start today.

errors.explanation: Backshift: is → was (“the school was getting a new garden”).
A month later, “tomorrow” is wrong: the next day.
today → that day (the day she visited).

questions.prompt: On Monday, Pia said, “I’ll bring cookies tomorrow.” On Friday, you report it. Which is correct?

options.text: Pia said that she would bring cookies tomorrow.
Pia said that she would bring cookies the next day.
Pia said that she will bring cookies tomorrow.

questions.explanation: On Friday, “tomorrow” would mean Saturday. Pia meant Tuesday: the next day.

questions.prompt: Which word replaces “here” when you report the words somewhere else?
questions.explanation: here → there. (now → then, this → that.)

questions.prompt: Last month Ravi said, “I visited my aunt two days ago.” Ravi said that he had visited his aunt…
questions.explanation: ago → before: two days before he spoke.

questions.prompt: At breakfast Mom says, “I’ll pick you up today.” At lunch, you tell a friend. Which is fine?

options.text: Mom said she would pick me up today.
Mom said she will pick me up yesterday.
Mom said I would pick her up today.

questions.explanation: It’s still the same day, so “today” can stay.

title: Pass on the message
prompt: Last Saturday your aunt left this voicemail for your family: “Hi, it’s Aunt Rosa! I’m coming to visit tomorrow. I will bring my famous lemon cake. Can you meet me at the train station at noon? I’ll wait for you by the ticket office. Don’t be late, because my phone battery is almost dead!” Today is Wednesday, and your mom asks what the message said. Write what you tell her (5–8 sentences) in reported speech, with no quotation marks. Shift the pronouns, the verbs, and the time and place words.
tips: Statement: Aunt Rosa said that she was coming to visit the next day.
Her question: She asked if we could meet her…
Her instruction: She told us not to be late.

title: Back to the exact words
instructions: Turn the reported speech back into direct speech. Add quotation marks, change the pronouns back and undo the backshift. Watch the task for where the tag goes.

items.task: Write Mia’s exact words, with the tag first.
items.source: Mia said that she was nervous.
items.explanation: Mia said, “I am nervous.” (or “I’m nervous.”)

items.task: Write Leo’s exact words, with the tag after. (He was talking to us.)
items.source: Leo said that he would help us.
hints: he → I, would → will, us → you.
End the quote with a comma: “…,” Leo said.
items.explanation: “I will help you,” Leo said.

items.task: Write Ana’s question, with the tag after. (She asked me.)
items.source: Ana asked if I was hungry.
hints: It’s a question again: question order.
items.explanation: “Are you hungry?” Ana asked. The question mark comes back.

items.task: Write Coach’s command, with the tag first.
items.source: Coach told us to run two laps.
hints: A command starts with the verb.
items.explanation: Coach said, “Run two laps.” A command starts with the verb.

items.task: Write Grandpa’s exact words, with the tag after.
items.source: Grandpa said that he had grown up on a farm.
answers: “I grew up on a farm,” Grandpa said.
“I grew up on a farm,” said Grandpa.
items.explanation: “I grew up on a farm,” Grandpa said. Had grown → grew.

title: Quote or paraphrase?
instructions: Does the essay sentence quote the source’s exact words, or paraphrase (report the idea in its own words)?

items.text: The author writes, “Every forest has a memory.”
According to Dr. Lee, “Sleep is the brain’s cleaning crew.”
The narrator calls the city “a maze of light.”
The article states, “Over 40% of food is wasted.”
The author explains that forests remember past fires.
Dr. Lee says that sleep helps clean the brain.
The article reports that almost half of all food is thrown away.
The narrator suggests that the city is confusing at night.

questions.prompt: Which sentence introduces a quote best?

options.text: “Dogs can sense when people are afraid.” That is interesting.
According to Dr. Ames, “Dogs can sense when people are afraid.”
Dogs. “Can sense when people are afraid.”

questions.explanation: “According to Dr. Ames” tells the reader who said it before the quote begins.

questions.prompt: In an essay, which lead-in usually fits best for what a book or article says?
questions.explanation: Essays usually talk about texts in the present tense: the author writes, states, explains.

questions.prompt: When is a paraphrase better than a quote?

options.text: When the idea matters but the exact words are long or plain
When the words are powerful or surprising

questions.explanation: Quote the striking words; paraphrase the useful ideas. Name the source either way.

questions.prompt: In a strong paragraph, what should come right after a quote?

options.text: Your explanation of what the quote shows
Nothing: the quote speaks for itself.

questions.explanation: The quote sandwich: lead-in, quote, then your explanation.

questions.prompt: Which is punctuated correctly?

options.text: The author writes “The sea was angry”.
The author writes, “The sea was angry.”
The author writes, “the sea was angry.”

questions.explanation: The same rules as dialogue: a comma after the lead-in, a capital, and the full stop inside.

title: Should school start later?
prompt: Read this short article. “Should school start later? Dr. Ana Ruiz, a sleep scientist, says that most teenagers’ body clocks shift during puberty. ‘Asking a thirteen-year-old to be alert at 7:30 a.m. is like asking an adult to be alert at 5:30,’ she explains. One district that moved its start time to 8:30 saw attendance rise by 8%.” Now write one paragraph (5–8 sentences) that answers the question: Should our school start later? Quote Dr. Ruiz once, with a lead-in. Report one other idea from the article in your own words. Explain what each piece of evidence shows.
tips: Lead-in for the quote: According to Dr. Ruiz, “…” or Dr. Ruiz explains, “…”
Paraphrase: The article reports that attendance went up in one district after school started later.
After each piece of evidence, explain it: This shows that…

title: Direct & Indirect Speech check
instructions: Ten questions on everything in this unit. You need 8 or more right (80%) to pass. If you don’t pass, you’ll see what to review and get new questions to try again.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
questions.explanation: Comma after the tag, capital to start, full stop inside the closing marks.

questions.prompt: “That’s my seat___ said Owen. What fills the gap?
questions.explanation: The sentence goes on into the tag, so a comma, and it goes inside the closing mark.

questions.prompt: Which question is punctuated correctly?
questions.explanation: The question mark goes inside, and it replaces the comma.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is correct?
questions.explanation: Exact words need quotation marks, and a quoted sentence starts with a capital.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is correct?
questions.explanation: The exclamation mark goes inside, and the tag starts with a small letter.

questions.prompt: Which split quote is correct?
questions.explanation: One sentence split by the tag: commas on both sides, and the second part starts with a small letter.

questions.prompt: Which is correct?
questions.explanation: “I’m done” and “Let’s go” are two sentences, so the tag ends with a full stop and “Let’s” gets a capital.

questions.prompt: When should you start a new paragraph in dialogue?

options.text: Every time a new person speaks
Only at the end of the conversation

questions.explanation: New speaker, new line.

questions.prompt: Which tag best shows that someone spoke quietly?
questions.explanation: “Whispered” tells the reader how the words were spoken.

questions.prompt: Ella said, “I am sick.” Which is the reported version?

options.text: Ella said that she was sick.
Ella said that I am sick.

questions.explanation: I → she, am → was, and no quotation marks.

questions.prompt: Max said to you, “I will call you.” Which is the reported version?

options.text: Max said that he would call me.
Max said that I will call you.
Max said that he will call you.

questions.explanation: I → he, you → me, will → would.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is reported speech?

options.text: Sam said that they had won.

questions.explanation: Reported speech has no quotation marks and changes the pronouns and verb.

questions.prompt: “We have finished,” the girls said. → The girls said that they ___ finished.
questions.explanation: have → had: one step back.

questions.prompt: “Where do you live?” Ana asked me. Which report is correct?

options.text: Ana asked me where I lived.
Ana asked me where did I live.
Ana asked me where I lived?

questions.explanation: Statement order, no “did”, and a full stop.

questions.prompt: “Is it raining?” asked Leo. Which report is correct?

options.text: Leo asked if it was raining.
Leo asked if was it raining.

questions.explanation: if + statement order: it was raining.

questions.prompt: “Stand up,” the coach said to us. Which report is correct?

options.text: The coach told us stand up.
The coach told us to stand up.
The coach told us standing up.

questions.explanation: A command: told + the person + to + the verb.

questions.prompt: “Don’t open the box,” Mom told me. Which report is correct?

options.text: Mom told me not to open the box.
Mom told me don’t open the box.
Mom told me to don’t open the box.

questions.explanation: “Don’t” becomes “not to”.

questions.prompt: On Monday Nia said, “I’ll finish it tomorrow.” On Friday: Nia said that she would finish it ___.
questions.explanation: tomorrow → the next day (Tuesday, not Saturday).

questions.prompt: At the park, Ben said, “I left my coat here.” Back at school: Ben said that he had left his coat ___.
questions.explanation: here → there: you’re not at the park any more.

questions.prompt: Last week Tam said, “I saw the movie yesterday.” Tam said that he had seen the movie ___.
questions.explanation: yesterday → the day before.

questions.prompt: Which word replaces “now” in reported speech?
questions.explanation: now → then.

questions.prompt: Which sentence introduces a quote best?

options.text: According to the author, “Oceans make half of our oxygen.”

questions.explanation: A lead-in (According to the author) tells readers where the words come from.

questions.prompt: Which lead-in usually fits an essay about a text?
questions.explanation: Essays discuss texts in the present tense: writes, states, explains.

questions.prompt: When should you paraphrase instead of quoting?

options.text: When the idea matters but the exact words don’t
When the words are striking or powerful

questions.explanation: Quote striking words; paraphrase useful ideas, and name the source either way.

title: School news story
prompt: Write a short news story (8–12 sentences) for the school website about an event: a bake sale, a science fair, a game or a field trip. Include at least two direct quotes from people who were there (one with the tag first, one with the tag after) and at least two sentences of reported speech, one of them a reported question or instruction. Start a new paragraph each time you quote a new person.
tips: Direct: Principal Cho said, “This was our best fair ever.” / “I’m coming back,” said Jae.
Reported: She said that the money would go to the library. Students asked if there would be another fair in the spring.
Check: commas and end marks inside the quotation marks; reported questions end with a full stop.
